amendments.summary: Kerala has not amended Section 138 (or ss.139-147) of the Negotiable Instruments Act - the offence, the presumptions, the notice period and limitation, and compounding are uniform central law, and Kerala adds nothing to that statute. What sits here instead are Kerala's own State Acts that bear on a s.138 case - chiefly the Kerala Police Act, 2011, which governs who serves process and executes the court's warrants. Also here is the Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, whose Article 21 fixes the court fee on a §138 complaint, appeal and revision. The rules of practice and e-filing rules are under State rules.

items.title: Kerala Police Act, 2011
items.note: A Kerala State Act - the police machinery a s.138 case relies on at the execution stage. A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case with no police investigation and no arrest at the outset; the police enter only when the court issues process, when the local Station House Officer executes a bailable or non-bailable warrant and serves court process. Rendered from the official clean text of the Act.

key.label: Functions of the police
key.note: The general duty of the police to serve court process and execute warrants - the point at which the police enter a s.138 case. There is no police investigation or arrest at the outset; they act only on the court's process once it issues.

items.title: Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959
items.cite: State Act · court fees on a §138 case
items.note: The State Act that fixes what it costs to bring and contest a cheque case in Kerala. The Kerala Finance Act, 2024 inserted Article 21 into Schedule II, setting the court fee on a §138 complaint (₹250 where the cheque is ≤ ₹10,000; otherwise 5% of the cheque amount, capped at ₹3 lakh), on an appeal (₹1,000 for the accused to the Sessions Court; half the trial-court fee for the complainant to the High Court) and on a revision (one-tenth of the cheque amount, or ₹1,500 for the accused). The slabs were revised again by the Finance Act, 2025 - verify the current figure before relying on it.

key.label: Court fee on a §138 complaint, appeal & revision
key.note: The ad valorem court fee that prices every stage of a Kerala cheque case - complaint, appeal and revision - scaled to the dishonoured-cheque amount. This is the filing economics a complainant meets before the case even begins.

rules.summary: How a Section 138 case is actually filed and tried in Kerala - the rules of practice and procedure a High Court or the State makes for its own courts (subsidiary legislation, made under an enabling Act). These sit on top of the uniform central offence and govern the form of process, service and the warrant ladder.

items.title: Criminal Rules of Practice, Kerala, 1982
items.note: The core state instrument for how a criminal court in Kerala signs, forms and serves process. Rules 7 to 14 cover summons to the accused and witnesses (police officers are summoned through their superior officer); Rule 13 sets the form; Rule 14 requires an English translation of process issued in Malayalam. Chapter III carries the absconding-accused track, and the Rules carry the forms and mechanics for warrants and for proclamation and attachment.

key.label: Signing & issue of summons
key.note: Who signs the summons to the accused and witnesses, and in whose name - the local mechanics behind issuing process on a s.138 complaint.

key.label: Form of summons
key.note: Prescribes the form the summons takes.

key.label: Translation of process
key.note: Process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation - the court-language rule biting on every summons and notice a s.138 case generates.

key.label: Absconding accused - proclamation & attachment
key.note: The warrant/absconder track: what the court does when the accused does not answer summons, escalating to proclamation and attachment of property - the far end of the summons -> warrant ladder in a s.138 case.

items.title: Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971
items.note: Govern the High Court's own side: appeals, revisions and criminal miscellaneous petitions, including quashing a s.138 complaint under s.482 CrPC / s.528 BNSS or a revision against conviction. A large share of Kerala s.138 litigation is the quashing and revision layer at the High Court.

key.label: Revision petitions
key.note: How a revision reaches the High Court - the route for a s.138 conviction or acquittal to be re-examined.

key.label: Procedure in criminal matters
key.note: The High Court's criminal-side procedure, including the quashing petitions under which many s.138 complaints are challenged.

items.title: Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala), 2021
items.note: The enabling rules for e-filing a complaint in Kerala courts. These govern how a s.138 complaint is filed, not how summons or warrants are served electronically.

key.label: Scope & applicability
key.note: Which courts and filings the e-filing regime covers - the gateway a s.138 complaint passes through when filed electronically.

key.label: Service through electronic means
key.note: When service by electronic means is permitted under the e-filing regime - the state's answer sits alongside the statutory modes of serving the demand notice and summons.

notifications.summary: Government orders, special-court notifications and standard operating procedures that shape how a §138 case is set up and run in Kerala - including the Kollam pilot court itself.

items.title: Special §138 Court at Kollam - 24×7 ON Court, 2024
items.note: The notification that stood up the Kollam pilot court itself. Issued under the proviso to section 9(1) BNSS and in consultation with the High Court, it establishes a dedicated Special Judicial Magistrate of the First Class at Kollam to try only §138 cheque cases, running as India's first 24×7 digital 'ON Court', with effect from 20 November 2024 (earlier sanctioned by G.O. 21/2024/Home dated 19 October 2024). This is the on-the-ground court the whole Kerala layer describes.

key.label: Establishment of the §138 Special Court (24×7 ON Court)
key.note: Creates a dedicated JMFC at Kollam to try only §138 cases as a 24×7 digital court, w.e.f. 20 November 2024. It is the court that hears the cheque case the rest of this layer feeds into - a concrete implementation of the summary-trial and special-court push for expeditious §138 disposal.

story.summary: How a §138 cheque-bounce case runs in Kerala, from filing to disposal - built purely from the rules and Acts, with every step citing the provision that governs it. Click any citation to open the exact text. This is the de jure process the black-letter rules prescribe; the lived, local practice is a separate layer.

process.summary: The procedural spine is the uniform national code (BNSS + the NI Act); Kerala's own rules operationalise each step. Where Kerala adds nothing, the step is pure central law.

timing.prescribed: Within 1 month of cause of action

steps.t: A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case: the payee or holder in due course files a written complaint, and the Magistrate can take cognizance only on such a complaint (never on a police report).
It must be filed within one month of the cause of action - which arises when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the demand notice served after dishonour.
In Kerala the complaint is e-filed through the DCMS portal under the E-Filing Rules, and the court fee is paid on filing.
The Magistrate examines the complainant (and any witnesses) on oath and, if satisfied there is ground to proceed, takes cognizance and issues process to the accused.
The summons is signed and issued by the court's ministerial officer 'by order of the Court', in the prescribed form.
Because the court language is Malayalam, process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation.
The summons is served in the manner the BNSS prescribes, and the NI Act's own mode of service also applies.
Service is effected through the police - the local Station House Officer serves the court's process. This is the only point at which the police enter a §138 case.
Where the e-filing regime permits, service may be by electronic means.

stages.stage: 4 · If the accused does not appear

steps.t: The court escalates up the warrant ladder: a warrant issues, and on continued absconding, proclamation and attachment of property.
Kerala's rules carry the absconding-accused track; the police execute the warrant.
The case is tried summarily, and the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit - the features that make §138 a fast-track offence.
A presumption operates in favour of the holder that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability, unless the accused rebuts it.
Kerala adds nothing procedural here - the summary-trial machinery is uniform central law.
On conviction the court may impose imprisonment up to two years and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, with compensation to the complainant.
The offence is compoundable: the parties may settle at any stage and the case is compounded, ending the prosecution.
The accused may appeal; the appellate court may require a deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine/compensation as a condition of the appeal.
A revision lies to the High Court, whose own rules govern its criminal side.
A complaint may also be challenged by a quashing petition before the High Court.
